title: Volunteering Abroad
description: A student describes the good and bad sides of volunteering in another country.
instructions: Read the student's account of volunteering abroad, then answer the questions. Choose the best answer for each question.

paragraphs.text: After finishing school, Hannah decided to take a gap year before starting university. She wanted to do something useful, so she joined a programme that sent young volunteers to teach English in a small village in Nepal. She spent four months there, living with a local family. Looking back, she says it was one of the most challenging and rewarding experiences of her life.

The first few weeks were difficult. Hannah did not speak the local language, and the food and daily routine were very different from home. There was no hot water, and the electricity often went off in the evening. She admits that she felt homesick and sometimes wanted to give up and fly back to England.

Slowly, however, things got better. Her host family was patient and taught her simple phrases, and the children at the school were eager to learn. Hannah became more confident in front of a class and learned to solve problems without help. She also made close friends with other volunteers from Canada, Germany and Brazil, and they still keep in touch.

Hannah is honest about the downsides of volunteering abroad. The programme was expensive, and she had to pay for her own flights and training. She also wonders whether a few months is long enough to make a real difference to the children's education. Even so, she would recommend the experience to others, as long as they choose a responsible organisation and go with realistic expectations.

Hannah's doubts are shared by many people who work in international development. Some critics use the word 'voluntourism' to describe short trips that are more about the volunteer's own adventure than the needs of the local community. They point out that untrained volunteers sometimes do jobs that local people could do better, and could be paid for. In schools, children may also find it confusing when a new teacher arrives every few months. For these reasons, critics argue that good intentions alone are not enough.

So how can someone choose a responsible programme? Experts suggest asking a few simple questions before signing up. Does the organisation work closely with local people, and did the community itself ask for the project? Is there proper training before volunteers start? Where exactly does the money go? Volunteers should also think honestly about their own skills. Someone with experience in building, nursing or teaching may be able to help more than someone who simply wants to travel.

Now in her second year at university, Hannah is studying education and still keeps in contact with her host family through video calls. Last year she organised a charity run with her friends to raise money for new books for the village school, which the head teacher had asked for. She believes the trip changed her more than it changed the village, and she is comfortable admitting that. Her advice to anyone who is thinking of volunteering is to research programmes carefully, to go with the aim of learning as well as helping, and to be honest about what they can really offer.
